item.title: Big Read: Zanzibar's hotels have five weeks to install CCTV. Nobody has produced the order.
item.description: Three accounts published in two days gave the archipelago's hotels a 15 December deadline, a camera specification and a schedule of penalties. None of them cites a circular, a gazette notice or a named official, and they disagree on the one question that decides the price.

item.title: Big Read: Zanzibar's hotels will argue about the 30 per cent. The expensive word in the order is "contract".
item.description: On 31 October Zanzibar raised its private sector wage floor by about 30 per cent from 1 January and lifted the dollar floor for foreign workers by half. In the same announcement the Labour Commissioner was told to put every private sector worker on a written contract by December. Over the twelve months to October the islands' advertised room rate fell about 18 per cent.

item.title: Big Read: The Mara's bed ceiling is absolute on paper. Nobody has got a court to look at it.
item.description: W Hospitality Group's new pipeline report names the Maasai Mara and the Serengeti among sub-Saharan Africa's luxury development hotspots, and asks whether they can absorb the supply. Kenya's own management plan answered that question in 2023. The answers that have actually counted since then have all been procedural.

item.title: Big Read: Four governments have read Tanzania's year. Not one of them has read it lately.
item.description: Tanzania went to London this week to sell eight million tourists, then a court in Dar es Salaam jailed the opposition leader. The commercial problem is not the verdict: it is that the four advisory pages which price that risk have all stopped being updated.

item.title: Big Read: East Africa is building hotel rooms for 29 days of football
item.description: AFCON 2027 is being sold to East African hoteliers as a demand event. The document that will decide who earns from it is a procurement specification, and it lands on the opening weeks of the region's most expensive season.

item.title: Big Read: Kenya made a health policy a condition of entry. A month in, Nairobi's biggest hospitals were not taking it.
item.description: Since 5 October every short-stay visitor to Kenya has had to buy a state-channelled US$50,000 travel health policy that the High Court has now upheld, and the cost to operators is not the US$48 but the fact that the country's own travel agents are telling members to keep buying private cover on top of it.

item.title: Big Read: East Africa spent 2026 adding charges to the room. A platform has started taking a cut of them.
item.description: Booking.com has moved government taxes into the base on which it calculates commission. The Caribbean has spent six months fighting it and won carve-outs for others. East Africa, which has layered more levies onto the room this year than any region on the continent, has not asked a single question.

item.title: Big Read: The world's largest seller of hotel rooms guided its next quarter down to 1 per cent. It did not blame the room.
item.description: Booking Holdings reported 7 per cent room-night growth on 3 November and told the market to expect 1 to 3 per cent in the fourth quarter, naming elevated airfares and reduced route capacity on long-haul routes as the cause. East Africa sells almost nothing but long-haul. The same month's aviation data shows African carriers adding international capacity faster than they fill it, at the lowest load

item.title: Big Read: Europe put a clock on the money your lodge pays back. Nobody set one on the money it is owed.
item.description: A statutory instrument laid in Westminster and a directive signed in Brussels have both written a refund deadline into the supplier's side of the package holiday contract, 14 days in Britain from April 2027 and seven days under EU law. Neither says a word about when the supplier gets paid in the first place. East Africa is signing the contracts that cross those dates right now.

item.title: Big Read: East Africa sells 2027 in three days at ExCeL. The hard part is getting into the room.
item.description: World Travel Market opens in London on Tuesday with Africa back on the main exhibition floor and eight East African businesses sharing one association stand. A year ago, 12 of the 14 Ugandan operators who had paid for space were refused UK visas, and no regional board has yet published what it spends to be in that building or what it brings home.
